meta.blurb: A monk spent about eight years in a garden counting peas, and the numbers kept landing near three to one. Gregor Mendel's own paper shows how he found a hidden rule of inheritance, and how it lay forgotten until 1900.
meta.bible: Gregor Mendel: an Augustinian monk and teacher in the town of Brünn (now Brno, in the Czech Republic); patient, careful and modest; he read his paper in 1865 and it was printed in 1866; abbot from 1868; died 1884. The Natural History Society of Brünn: the audience for his two lectures. Pisum: the garden pea, his main plant. Phaseolus: the bean plants he also crossed. Hieracium: hawkweed, which behaved differently. Kölreuter and Gärtner: earlier breeders of hybrids; Carl Nägeli: the botanist who answered his letters. Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak: the three scientists who found his paper again in 1900. Key terms: Hybrid, Generation, Dominant, Recessive, Pollen, Anthers, Pistil, Ratio, Genes, Gene, Chromosomes, DNA, Genetics, Segregation, Independent Assortment, Abbot, Monastery. Facts: seven pairs of features (seed shape round or wrinkled; seed colour yellow or green; seed coat grey-brown or white; pod shape full or pinched; unripe pod colour green or yellow; flowers along the stem or at its tip; plant height tall or short); 34 kinds of pea tested, 22 kept; about eight years of experiments; second generation counts 5,474 round to 1,850 wrinkled, 6,022 yellow to 2,001 green, 787 tall to 277 short; two features together: 556 seeds in four groups of 315, 101, 108 and 32, close to 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; the word gene came long after Mendel. Voice and tone: clear, patient and warm, a scientist's paper told step by step; the numbers are real; where he was uncertain, the text says so.

B1B2: Gregor Mendel was a monk who lived in the town of Brünn, which is now Brno in the Czech Republic. In the monastery garden, he began a long series of experiments with plants.
People had been crossing plants to make new kinds for a long time. Yet nobody had found a general law that said what the young plants would look like.
Mendel wanted to find out the law by which hybrids are formed. He knew that this would take years of patient work with thousands of plants.

Mendel chose the garden pea for several good reasons, which he explains clearly. Its plants have clear differences that are easy to see, they grow easily, and their young plants can be raised in large numbers.

In a pea flower, two petals form a small boat that closes around the parts that make pollen and seed. Normally the flower fertilises itself before it opens, so pollen from other plants almost never gets in.
Mendel got 34 kinds of pea from seed sellers and grew them for two years to test them. He kept 22 kinds that always produced young plants just like their parents.
Mendel studied seven features, and each came in two clear forms. The first was the shape of the seed, which was round or wrinkled, and the second was its colour, yellow or green.
Three more features were the colour of the seed coat, grey-brown or white, and the shape of the ripe pod, which was swollen or pinched. Another was the colour of the unripe pod, green or yellow.
The last two features were the place of the flowers, along the stem or at its tip, and the height of the plant. The tall plants were much taller than the short ones, which stayed small.
The work took about eight years and covered many thousands of plants. Mendel counted every plant and every seed, and he wrote down each result.
To cross two plants, Mendel opened a young flower before its pollen was ripe. With small tweezers he removed the parts that make pollen, so the flower could not fertilise itself.
Next, he brushed pollen from the other plant onto the flower. Then he covered it with a small bag, so that no insect could bring in pollen by mistake.
Mendel crossed the plants both ways, using each as the pollen parent in turn. The results were the same, so the father plant and the mother plant seem to give equal shares.
When Mendel crossed a round-seeded plant with a wrinkled-seeded one, all the seeds of the first generation were round. The wrinkled shape seemed to have disappeared from the plants completely.
Mendel called the feature that showed in the hybrids dominant, and the feature that hid he called recessive. The word recessive means that it steps back and waits.
The same thing happened with every one of the seven pairs of features. Grey-brown seed coats, full pods, green pods, flowers along the stem and tall plants were all dominant.
Next, Mendel let the hybrid plants fertilise themselves and grew their seeds. The hidden wrinkled shape had not been lost, and it came back in some of the new plants.
In one experiment, Mendel counted 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled ones. There were about three round seeds for each wrinkled one.
With seed colour, he counted 6,022 yellow seeds and 2,001 green ones. That is again very close to a ratio of three to one.
The other five features gave almost the same result. In the experiment on height, for example, there were 787 tall plants and 277 short ones.
The ratio is never perfect, because chance plays a part. Mendel saw that the more plants he counted, the closer the results came to three to one.
Next, Mendel grew the seeds of each second-generation plant separately. The plants with the hidden feature, such as wrinkled seeds, always produced offspring just like themselves.
Among the plants that showed the dominant feature, about one in three always bred true. The other two in three were hybrids and gave both kinds of young plants again.
This means that the second generation contains three kinds of plant. One quarter are pure dominant, one half are hybrid, and one quarter are pure recessive.
To show the pattern, Mendel wrote the dominant form as A and the hidden form as a. Pure plants are then A or a, and the hybrid has both, written Aa.
Mendel explained the pattern with a bold and very simple idea. A hybrid makes two kinds of pollen and two kinds of egg cells in equal numbers, and each cell carries only one form.

Imagine tossing two coins together many times, and counting how often you get two heads, a head and a tail, or two tails. The three results come up in the ratio one to two to one, and Mendel's plants follow the same law of chance.
Mendel tested his explanation by crossing hybrids back with a pure plant of the hidden kind. His idea predicted equal numbers of the two kinds, and that is just what he found.
Next, Mendel studied two different features at the very same time. He crossed plants with round yellow seeds with plants with wrinkled green seeds.
All the seeds of the first generation were round and yellow, which are the two dominant forms. The hybrids carried the hidden features without showing them.
The 556 seeds that Mendel counted fell into four different groups. There were 315 round yellow seeds, 101 wrinkled yellow, 108 round green and 32 wrinkled green.
The new combinations showed that shape and colour are passed on separately. A seed can be round and green, or wrinkled and yellow, just by chance.
The four groups appeared in a ratio close to nine, three, three and one. If you count one feature alone, you still get three to one: 423 round seeds against 133 wrinkled ones.
Mendel then went on to follow three features at the same time. By his rule there should be 27 different kinds of plant in the second generation, and his results agreed with this.
If you follow all seven features at once, there are 2,187 possible kinds of plant. That is how a few simple rules can make nature so rich in variety.
Mendel's idea can be put simply: a plant carries a pair of hidden factors for each feature, one from each parent. Scientists later gave these hidden factors the name genes, a word Mendel never used.

Mendel also crossed beans, plants that belong to a group called Phaseolus. Their flower colours gave much more complicated results, and he suggested that several colour factors might be working together.
Mendel knew that not every plant behaved like his peas. Hawkweed, for example, seemed to follow different rules, and he could not explain why.
Earlier breeders such as Kölreuter and Gärtner had done careful work with hybrids. However, they looked at the whole plant instead of single features, and they did not count the offspring.
Looked at closely, Mendel's method was simple but quite new. He chose clear features, crossed his plants with care, followed each generation separately and counted every result.
Mendel's work shows that a plant can look like one parent and still carry the hidden form of the other. How a living thing looks does not tell us everything about what it carries.
In his last pages, Mendel asks what hybrids might teach us about how new forms of plants arise. He is careful, however, and says that more experiments are needed before anyone can be sure.
In February and March of 1865, Mendel read his paper aloud to the Natural History Society of Brünn. It was printed in the society's journal the next year, in 1866.
At first, almost nobody paid attention to the paper. Mendel wrote to a well-known botanist named Nägeli, but he did not receive the help or the agreement he hoped for.
In 1868, Mendel was chosen to lead his monastery, and his new duties left little time for experiments. He died in 1884, without knowing how famous his paper would become.

In 1900, scientists in three countries were running similar experiments and found the same ratios. When they searched the old books, they discovered that Mendel had explained it all thirty-five years before.
A few years later, the new science was given the name genetics. Scientists soon found that the hidden factors, now called genes, lie on tiny threads inside cells called chromosomes.
Later work showed that genes lying close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together. Mendel's seven features happened to behave independently, which made his rules easy to see.
Students in many countries still repeat Mendel's experiments with peas. His two main findings are known today as the law of segregation and the law of independent assortment.
Mendel's garden was small, and his tools were simple: a brush, a notebook and a great deal of patience. With them, he found a law of nature that still helps us to understand every living thing.
C1C2: In the garden of an old monastery in the town of Brünn, now called Brno, the monk Gregor Mendel began a series of experiments that would take many years of patient work. His paper, read to a small scientific society in 1865, describes how he crossed different kinds of plants and counted what grew. Few people who heard it could have guessed that it was laying the foundation of a new science.

Gardeners and scientists had been crossing different plants for generations, hoping to create new varieties or to learn how living things pass on their features. Yet, as Mendel observes, no one had found a general law that could say in advance what the offspring of such a cross would look like. He thought the reason was plain: nobody had yet carried out enough careful experiments, over enough years, on enough plants.

Mendel set himself a clear goal: to discover the general law by which hybrid plants are formed and by which their features pass to the next generation. He knew that the task was a large one that could only be settled by long, patient work on a very great number of plants. The man who would succeed, he saw, must be willing to count, to wait and to repeat his work many times.

Mendel chose the garden pea for several good reasons, each of which made his experiments easier and more reliable. Its varieties differ in clear features that are easy to tell apart, its flowers are shaped so that foreign pollen rarely gets in, and its hybrids are fertile, so that they can go on to produce more plants. Few other plants, he judged, offered so many advantages at once, which is why the humble pea became so famous.

The pea flower is built like a little closed boat, in which two petals wrap tightly around the parts that make pollen and seeds. Before the flower even opens, it has usually fertilised itself, which keeps out pollen carried by insects and the wind. Mendel could therefore trust that a plant he left alone would pass its features on in a pure and predictable way.

Mendel obtained thirty-four kinds of pea from seed dealers and tested each of them in his garden for two years. Only those that always produced offspring exactly like themselves, generation after generation, were good enough for his purpose, and he kept twenty-two. From these carefully chosen plants he would draw all the pairs of features that made his experiments possible.

Mendel focused on seven features of the pea plant, each of which came in two sharply different forms, with nothing in between. The first was the shape of the ripe seed, either smooth and round or wrinkled and angular, and the second was the colour of the seed's inside, either yellow or green. A pea was either one thing or the other, which made every plant easy to count.

Three further features concerned the seed coat, which was either grey-brown or white, and the ripe pod, which was either full and swollen or tightly pinched between the seeds. The unripe pod supplied a third pair of forms, being either green or yellow. Each pair was clear enough that Mendel could classify a plant at a glance, without any doubt.

The last two features were where the flowers grew, either along the stem or bunched at its tip, and the height of the plant. Tall plants reached about two metres, while the short ones stayed below half a metre, a difference so large that it could never be mistaken. Altogether Mendel now had seven separate pairs of features to follow carefully through all the generations of his experiments.

Altogether the experiments lasted about eight years, and they involved many thousands of plants that Mendel grew, examined and counted one by one. He recorded each result in a notebook, and he never trusted a pattern until the numbers had grown large enough to support it. Such patient counting, unusual in biology at the time, was the secret of his success.

To make a cross, Mendel opened a young flower bud before its pollen was ripe and carefully cut away the parts that make pollen. This stopped the flower from fertilising itself, so that it could be pollinated only by the plant that he chose. The work needed a steady hand and a good deal of patience, for the buds were small and delicate.

Next, he took pollen from the plant he wished to use as the father and dusted it onto the prepared flower with a fine brush. He then covered the flower so that no insect could bring unwanted pollen, and later he gathered the seeds that grew. Every one of those seeds was known to be the child of exactly the two plants he had chosen.

Mendel took care to cross his plants in both directions, using a given plant sometimes as the source of pollen and sometimes as the receiver of it. The results were exactly the same either way, which showed that the pollen parent and the seed parent make equal contributions to the next generation. It was an important clue that nothing in the experiment depended on which plant played which part.

When he crossed a plant with round seeds and a plant with wrinkled seeds, every seed of the first generation turned out to be round. The hybrids did not look like a blend of their parents, as one might have expected, but resembled just one of them. The wrinkled shape, which had been so plain in one of the parents, had apparently vanished without leaving any trace.

Mendel gave names to the two kinds of feature: the one that appears in the hybrid he called dominant, and the one that is hidden he called recessive. Round seeds were dominant over wrinkled, and yellow seeds over green, while the hidden forms were merely waiting out of sight. The words he chose have lasted a century and a half, and they are still used in every school that teaches genetics.

The same result appeared in all seven pairs of features, whichever pair Mendel chose to study. Grey-brown seed coats, full pods, green pods, flowers along the stem and tall plants all proved to be dominant over their opposites, just as round and yellow seeds had been. In every case the first generation of hybrids looked exactly like one of the two parents.

In the next step, Mendel allowed the hybrid plants to fertilise themselves and then sowed their seeds. The feature that had vanished in the first generation, such as the wrinkled shape, reappeared in a portion of the grandchildren, as fresh and clear as it had been in the grandparents. It had not been lost or blended away in the hybrid, as many had supposed, but had simply been hidden from view.

Mendel did not simply note that the hidden feature had returned, but counted exactly how many plants showed each form. From one experiment on seed shape he reported 5,474 round seeds and 1,850 wrinkled ones, which is about three round seeds for every wrinkled one. The numbers were clearly not random, and they begged for an explanation that nobody had yet been able to give.

Another experiment gave the same pattern in a different feature: Mendel counted 6,022 yellow seeds and 2,001 green ones. The ratio is again very close to three to one, though not exactly so, as it would not be in any real count of living things. Something regular and orderly, it seemed, lay hidden behind these figures, waiting for someone to explain it.

The five remaining features behaved in just the same way, each giving a ratio that came close to three to one. In the experiment on height, for example, Mendel counted 787 tall plants and 277 short ones, and the other pairs gave similarly consistent figures. A pattern that held across seven quite unrelated features of the same plant could hardly be an accident of chance.

Real counts of living things are never perfectly neat, and Mendel knew that chance plays a part in every fertilisation. He saw that the ratios came nearer to three to one as the number of plants grew, just as a coin tossed a few times may give uneven results but tossed a thousand times comes close to half heads. This is why his work needed so many thousands of plants, and why a smaller experiment might easily have missed the pattern.

To understand the second generation better, Mendel grew the seeds of each plant separately and watched the third generation come up. Those plants that showed the hidden feature, such as wrinkled seeds, always produced offspring exactly like themselves, however many times he repeated the process. They were as pure as the original wrinkled parents had been, and in the generations he tested they stayed that way.

The plants showing the dominant feature were not all alike, for when Mendel tested them, about one in three always bred true. The other two in three were hybrids, which gave a second generation that showed both the dominant and the hidden feature in the familiar ratio of three to one. Hidden beneath the same outward appearance, therefore, were two quite different kinds of plant, one pure and one mixed.

The tallies pointed to a striking conclusion: the second generation consists of three distinct kinds of plant, and not merely two. A quarter are pure for the dominant feature, a half are hybrids, and a quarter are pure for the hidden one, giving the proportion one to two to one. Since the hybrids resemble the dominant plants, this underlying pattern is disguised as the apparent ratio of three to one.

To make the pattern easy to see, Mendel used letters, writing the dominant form as A and the hidden form as a. A pure dominant plant is then A, a pure hidden one is a, and a hybrid carries both, which he could write as Aa. When two hybrids are crossed, the offspring come out in the pattern A, two Aa and a, the very series of one, two and one that his counting had found.

Mendel's explanation was bold and beautifully simple: a hybrid plant forms two kinds of pollen and two kinds of egg cells, in equal numbers, and each cell carries only one of the two forms of the feature. The pairing of the two parents' cells at fertilisation then happens at random, in the way that any one of several possibilities occurs by chance. The mixture of forms in the hybrid is therefore a pairing, not a blending.

A coin can show how this works: if two coins are tossed together many times, two heads, one of each, or two tails turn up in the ratio one to two to one. In the same way, when pollen and egg cells of a hybrid meet at random, the four possible pairings appear in equal numbers, which gives one pure dominant, two hybrids and one pure hidden type. This simple link between the laws of chance and the facts of inheritance was the very heart of Mendel's explanation.

A good idea should predict something new, and Mendel checked his by crossing hybrids with plants of the pure parent forms. If the hybrids really made two kinds of cell in equal numbers, the offspring should appear in about equal numbers of two kinds, and his experiments gave results that agreed closely. The prediction could easily have failed, which makes its success all the more convincing to anyone who reads the paper today.

Having understood single features, Mendel went on to follow two at once, to find out whether they travelled together or separately. He crossed plants with round yellow seeds with plants that had wrinkled green ones, and then waited to see what the hybrids would produce. The answer would show whether a feature was inherited as part of a package or entirely on its own.

Every seed of the first generation was round and yellow, because these were the two dominant forms, and the hybrids therefore showed no sign of the wrinkled or green features they were carrying. When Mendel sowed those seeds and allowed the plants to fertilise themselves, however, the next generation brought a rich variety of forms. In all, he gathered and counted 556 seeds from these plants, and then he began the careful work of sorting them.

Mendel sorted the 556 seeds into four groups: 315 were round and yellow, 101 were wrinkled and yellow, 108 were round and green, and 32 were wrinkled and green. Two of these combinations, wrinkled yellow and round green, had never appeared in either of the original plants. The features had been shuffled like a pack of cards and dealt out again, quite separately, in entirely new hands.

The appearance of new combinations proved that the features were inherited independently of one another, so that the shape of a seed told one nothing about its colour. Each feature seemed to be shuffled and dealt out separately, as though governed by its own private lottery. This was the second great discovery of the paper, after the three-to-one ratio itself.

The four groups appeared in a ratio close to nine to three to three to one, which is exactly what chance would give if each feature were shuffled on its own. Counted separately, each feature still showed the old three to one: 423 round seeds against 133 wrinkled ones, and 416 yellow against 140 green. The old rule had not been overturned but widened to cover two features at once.

Mendel went on to follow three features at once, which made the pattern even more intricate. According to his rule there should be twenty-seven different kinds of plant in the second generation, and the results he obtained agreed well with that expectation. The more features that are combined, the more varied the offspring become, though the same simple rule governs each of them.

If all seven features were followed together, Mendel's rule predicts that 2,187 different kinds of plant could appear in the second generation, a number that grows swiftly with each extra feature. Out of so few simple pairs of features, therefore, the shuffling of cells can produce a bewildering variety of offspring. This helps to explain why the children in one family can look so different from each other.

Put in modern words, Mendel's central idea is that every plant carries a pair of hidden factors for each feature, one received from each parent, and that these two factors separate when new pollen and egg cells are made. He did not know what such factors were made of, or where they were kept, and the word gene was not invented until long after his death. Yet his reasoning was so sound that the discoveries made after his death fitted it closely, and often confirmed it.

Mendel also crossed beans, plants of the kind called Phaseolus, and here the results were harder to read. The flower colours did not follow the simple three-to-one pattern, and he suggested that several separate factors for colour might be working together to produce the shades he saw. It was a hint, many years ahead of its time, that some features depend on more than one factor.

Mendel was honest about the limits of his work, and he admitted that not every plant behaved like his peas. Hawkweed, with which he was also experimenting, gave results that seemed to follow quite different rules, and he could not yet explain why. We now know that hawkweed can make seeds without fertilisation, but that discovery lay far in the future.

Mendel gave credit to earlier breeders such as Joseph Kölreuter and Carl Friedrich Gärtner, who had carried out a great many crosses with real care. Their attention, however, was fixed on the plant as a whole, whereas Mendel followed one single feature at a time, kept the generations apart, and above all counted the offspring. In that change of method lay the whole difference between a collection of observations and a law.

Looked at closely, Mendel's method was both simple and new: he chose features with clear alternatives, crossed his plants under control, followed each generation separately and counted every result. Because the questions he asked had definite numerical answers, nature could answer them without ambiguity. That is the quality that makes the paper still a model of how to design an experiment.

One of the paper's quiet lessons is that two plants may look exactly alike and yet differ in what they carry within them. A hybrid with round seeds and a pure plant with round seeds are indistinguishable by eye, but their offspring reveal the difference at once. Appearance, in other words, is only the visible half of the story of inheritance.

In his closing remarks, Mendel wonders what his results might say about the way in which new forms of plants arise, a question much discussed in his time. He is cautious, however, and reminds his readers that conclusions drawn from peas alone should not be extended to all living things without further experiment. The caution was typical of the man, who preferred to trust his counted plants rather than speculation.

In February and March of 1865, Mendel presented his results in two lectures to the Natural History Society of Brünn, an audience of local naturalists and teachers. The paper was printed the following year in the society's proceedings, and copies were sent to libraries and to a number of scholars. Nothing about the occasion suggested that it would later be counted among the great moments in the history of science.

At first the paper attracted very little attention, and the scientists who did read it seem not to have grasped how much it meant. Mendel exchanged letters with the well-known botanist Carl Nägeli, who was not convinced and who urged him to try other plants, such as hawkweed, which turned out to behave quite differently. The work went on, but the world of science was not yet ready to listen.

In 1868 Mendel was elected abbot of his monastery, and the demands of that office left him little time for the garden. He continued to observe the weather and the plants around him until his death in 1884, with no idea that his pea experiments would one day be placed among the foundations of modern biology. The quiet monk was a scientist whose reputation was made entirely after he was gone.

In 1900, three scientists working separately in different countries, Hugo de Vries, Carl Correns and Erich von Tschermak, obtained results very like Mendel's and then found his forgotten paper in the library. They saw at once that he had reached the same laws thirty-five years before them, with a clarity that they could hardly match. From that moment, the work of the monk of Brünn began to be read all over the world.

Within a few years the new science received the name genetics, and researchers began to look for the physical basis of Mendel's hidden factors. They found that these factors, now called genes, lie along tiny threads inside the cell called chromosomes, which are shared out between pollen and egg cells in exactly the way that his reasoning required. Later still, in the middle of the twentieth century, scientists learned that genes are made of a chemical called DNA.

Mendel's rules are not the whole of heredity, and later research showed some important exceptions. Genes that lie close together on the same chromosome tend to be inherited together, and many features depend on several genes working together, as the beans had hinted. Yet the seven features Mendel chose happened to behave independently, which made the basic laws clear enough to find.

In classrooms around the world, students still grow and count peas as Mendel did, and the three-to-one ratio still appears on the page. His two chief findings are now known as the law of segregation, which says that the two factors of a pair separate when cells are made, and the law of independent assortment, which says that different pairs are shuffled separately. Few discoveries in biology have been so easy to repeat, or so quickly understood by a beginner.

Mendel's garden was small and his equipment was simple, no more than a brush, some bags, a notebook and a great deal of patience. With those modest means he asked a clear question, counted the answer and found a law that helps us to understand every living thing, from the pea plant to ourselves. The lesson of his paper is that careful, honest experiments, repeated often enough, can reveal the hidden order beneath ordinary appearances.
